clue.text: Resort is in France, except for about one hotel

indicators.note: the word for except is placed around the letter for one

parts.note: bar, as a preposition, means except for
the Roman numeral for one is I
the Ritz is a famous luxury hotel

explanation.surface: A traveller's note that a French resort qualifies, bar a hotel or so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is in France' only places the resort: Biarritz is on the French Basque coast. 'about' puts I (one) inside BAR (except for).
explanation.definitionFit: Biarritz is a fashionable seaside holiday town in south-west France.

clue.text: Objections about dear foreign tradesmen

indicators.note: the objections are placed around the foreign word

parts.note: buts are objections, as in no ifs or buts
cher is the French for dear

explanation.surface: Complaints about expensive imported goods from shopkeepers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dear' suggests expensive, but it is the endearment, in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat sellers are shopkeepers, members of a trade.

clue.text: Losing a pound this, team would have no forwards

definitions.text: Losing a pound this, team would have no forwards

parts.words: Losing a pound this, team would have no forwards
parts.note: drop L, the pound sign, from the rugby team's name and what is left says it is all backs

explanation.surface: A rugby side that, after a weight loss, would lack a pack.
explanation.walkthrough: The New Zealand rugby team: take out L (pound) and you get ALL BACKS, a side with no forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The national rugby union side of New Zealand, named for its kit.

clue.text: Continue to produce rents in the 'city

parts.note: to rip is to tear, making rents
to go on is to continue

explanation.surface: Advice to keep tearing holes somewhere in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rents' looks like money paid; it means tears. Ripon is a small cathedral city in North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripon is a cathedral city in Yorkshire, England.

clue.text: Subjects are about right for hot places

indicators.note: the subjects are placed around the letter for right

parts.note: topics are subjects

explanation.surface: Discussion themes fit for warm countries.
explanation.definitionFit: The region either side of the equator is the world's hottest zone.

clue.text: Express opposition to something

explanation.surface: A dictionary-style note on how to protest about a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: To object is to raise a protest; an object is a thing, any item at all.

clue.text: Set speech given by coarse actors?

parts.note: broad humour is coarse
a cast is the actors in a play

explanation.surface: A prepared address delivered by vulgar players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set speech' looks like a prepared oration; the set is a wireless set, so speech heard on the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: A radio talk is speech transmitted over the air to a receiving set.

clue.text: Morayshire has the Spanish spirit

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: A Scottish county with a Spanish soul.
explanation.walkthrough: Elgin is the county town of Morayshire in north-east Scotland, which was itself once called Elginshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The county of Moray was formerly named Elginshire after its chief town.

clue.text: Well loaded vessel?

parts.note: a ship filled with what comes from an oil well, rather than one neatly packed

explanation.surface: A ship packed with care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like an adverb; it is an oil well.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship built to carry oil in bulk.

clue.text: Clean tyrant ?

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a dictator could be decent.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as de-spot, to remove spots, for the first sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove marks is to clean; an absolute ruler who abuses power is a tyrant.

clue.text: Make speech along familiar lines, perhaps

definitions.text: Make speech along familiar lines, perhaps

parts.words: Make speech along familiar lines, perhaps
parts.note: speaking along lines read literally as wires: talking down the cable that carries a call

explanation.surface: Advice to a speaker to stick to well-worn arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'familiar lines' suggests clichés; the lines are telegraph wires carrying a voice.
explanation.definitionFit: To ring someone up is to speak to them over a wire line.

clue.text: Might be playing a heart, for example

explanation.surface: A card player wondering whether a heart might be the lead.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-table picture misleads: the first sense is a church instrument that might be playing, the second a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: A church instrument with pipes might be playing music; the heart is one of the body's vital parts.

clue.text: The girl in the lending library?

indicators.note: the name sits inside the run of letters of these words

explanation.surface: Asking which young woman works at the library.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen is a woman's first name, so a girl.

clue.text: Unblushing cheek

parts.note: a face that does not redden, read as the brazen kind of cheek, sauciness shown without shame

explanation.surface: A pale face that never colours up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cheek' looks like part of the face; it is nerve or insolence, and the unblushing kind is shameless.
explanation.definitionFit: Shameless rudeness or effrontery is cheek of the most brazen sort.

clue.text: Game involving fraudulent money-making ?

explanation.surface: A sport that has got mixed up with swindling.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the indoor ball sport played against walls; the second is a crooked scheme for profit.
explanation.definitionFit: The court sport played with a bat and hard ball against walls; scams for illicit profit are also called this.

clue.text: Breakfast food provided in some of these cases

definitions.text: Breakfast food provided in some of these cases

parts.words: Breakfast food provided in some of these cases
parts.note: the cases are natural containers, each wrapping a morning meal

explanation.surface: A note that breakfast is served in some instances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cases' suggests instances; they are containers.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard shells of eggs enclose the food many eat at breakfast.

clue.text: Worthless attempt to surround the wood

indicators.note: the word for attempt is placed around the wood

parts.note: a try is an attempt
ash is a tree and its timber

explanation.surface: A doomed effort to encircle a forest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of rubbishy quality is of no value.

clue.text: Rash appears with some fever ?

explanation.surface: A skin rash that comes with a temperature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like the skin complaint; it means reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetuous people act rashly; with a fever the head feels hot.

clue.text: Sweets made of chopped pears contain nothing upsetting

indicators.note: the rearranged pears hold the other piece inside
the pears are cut up, their letters rearranged
in a down clue, upset means turned upwards, read backwards

parts.note: nil means nothing

explanation.surface: Confectionery of diced fruit with nothing to cause a tummy upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chopped' turns PEARS into PRAES; 'upsetting' turns NIL to LIN; 'contain' puts LIN inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Pralines are sweets of nuts in caramelised sugar.

clue.text: Customs of upper-class savants ?

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class speech and manners
sages are wise, learned people

explanation.surface: Wondering about the habits of posh intellectuals.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs are established practices or habits.

clue.text: A fine sort of candlestick

explanation.surface: Describing an elegant candle holder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine' looks like an adjective; it is a penalty: at Oxford colleges, a forfeit for a breach of table manners.
explanation.definitionFit: A forfeit imposed at an Oxford dinner is a penalty; a wall bracket holding candles is a lighting fixture.

clue.text: Turner appears unaltered by retirement

indicators.note: retirement is a going back, so the word read backwards stays the same

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An art note that a Turner painting survives the artist retiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' suggests the painter J. M. W. Turner; it means something that rotates.
explanation.definitionFit: A device or muscle that rotates something is a thing that turns.

clue.text: Official routine broken at Moscow sports ?

parts.note: Moscow stands for Soviet communism, whose colour is red

indicators.note: the letters are shuffled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
PE, physical education, is school sports

explanation.surface: Bureaucracy disrupted at a Moscow sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges AT and PE into TAPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Bureaucratic procedure is named for the ribbon once tied round official documents.

clue.text: Something depressing which might brighten our views

definitions.text: Something depressing which might brighten our views

parts.words: Something depressing which might brighten our views
parts.note: depressing in the sense of being pressed down, as a button is, to turn a light on

explanation.surface: A gloomy thing that could make us more cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'depressing' suggests gloomy; it is something pressed down.
explanation.definitionFit: A light control is pressed to turn the lamp on.

clue.text: Maxim repeater, perhaps

explanation.surface: A saying that someone keeps repeating.
explanation.walkthrough: A repeater is also a striking pocket watch, so this word could belong to one: a watch's word.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan or motto is a maxim; a watchword is something passed on and repeated by those who keep watch.

clue.text: Two anti-reformers carry point

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the point inside
re-forming the letters of the word means rearranging them

parts.note: W, west, is a compass point

explanation.surface: Two opponents of reform carrying a point of debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anti-reformers' reads as opponents of reform; split it: ANTI re-formed gives TAIN, and 'carry' puts W inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain is an old word for a pair.

clue.text: Charming bit of work?

explanation.surface: A pleasant stint of labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charming' looks like an adjective; it is the noun sense, the casting of a charm.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming means casting magic, as an enchantment does; a stint or period of work is also this.

clue.text: " Ithuriel with his" (Milton)

parts.note: a gap to fill from Paradise Lost, where the angel touches Satan with his weapon

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: In Paradise Lost Book IV, the angel Ithuriel touches the disguised Satan with his weapon, which reveals his true form.
explanation.definitionFit: A long pointed throwing weapon is what the angel carries in the poem.

clue.text: For Cromwell many a blemish is turned to provide net gain

indicators.note: the word for the blemish is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: a wart is a skin blemish
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword's usual many

explanation.surface: Cromwell's famous warts somehow turned to profit.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Cromwell asked to be painted 'warts and all', hence 'For Cromwell' setting up the blemish. 'is turned' makes TRAW from WART.
explanation.definitionFit: To drag a fishing net behind a boat is to haul in a catch.

clue.text: Type letters for a Dr Connel

indicators.note: the letters of the doctor's name are rearranged to give another word

explanation.surface: Typing up letters for a doctor called Connel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' looks like a verb; it is a noun, a typeface.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarendon is a heavy typeface, a style of printing letters.

clue.text: Dost 'engage in sharp practice ? Not this one

definitions.text: Dost 'engage in sharp practice ? Not this one

parts.words: Dost 'engage in sharp practice ? Not this one
parts.note: in old second-person verb form, thou who sharpen a blade says the same as the adjective; such a person would never cheat

explanation.surface: Asking whether thou cheatest, and answering that a decent person does not.
explanation.walkthrough: Archaic 'thou hon-est' means 'thou dost hone', sharpening; yet sharp practice is cheating, which an upright person avoids.
explanation.definitionFit: A truthful, upright person is the very opposite of someone who cheats.

clue.text: Waitresses go round free in these islands

indicators.note: the waitresses are placed around the word for free

parts.note: Hebe was the cupbearer of the gods, so hebes are waitresses
to rid is to free

explanation.surface: Waitresses walking about at liberty on a group of islands.
explanation.walkthrough: Hebe, cupbearer to the Greek gods, gives HEBES for waitresses. The Hebrides are islands off the west coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrides are an archipelago off western Scotland.
